However, another way that's been added into Horizon for players to add some cars into their collection is the new loyalty rewards program. This allows players who have played previous Forza titles, whether it was the Horizon entries or the Motorsport ones, to earn a select few cars. All of these cars are quite fast, and a nice gesture from the developers to show their appreciation for our loyalty to the franchise!

title: Rare disease diagnosis Q&A: Patrick's story
summary: Understanding the rare disease diagnostic odyssey.
body_text: Understanding a rare disease diagnosis: Patrick's story ‍ We recently connected with Sue Bresnahan, whose son Patrick was diagnosed with a rare, genetic disorder after genetic testing revealed a mutation in the CACNA1C gene. Like many parents facing unexplained symptoms like developmental delays or missed milestones, Sue endured a long diagnostic odyssey that was filled with specialist visits, emotional strain, and unanswered questions. It wasn’t until genetic testing was done that her family received a definitive diagnosis: a CACNA1C-related disorder, a rare condition that can affect neurological and cardiac function. In this conversation, Sue shares how genetic testing changed everything, from fear and isolation to advocacy and hope. Her story underscores why early and accessible genetic testing is critical for families navigating rare pediatric conditions. ‍ Plus, Sue’s story features an incredible dog named Yammy, and the world needs more stories about relationships like Patrick and Yammy’s. ‍ When did you first sense something was different with Patrick, and how did others respond to your concerns? I first sensed something was different with Patrick when he wasn’t hitting his developmental milestones on time. At three months old, he still had not rolled over, which concerned me right away. Every three months, I brought up my worries to the pediatrician and said clearly that something wasn’t right. In this pediatric practice, they assess developmental milestones every three months, and at each visit, Patrick consistently wasn’t meeting them. Despite this, I was often told I was looking at him with a fine-tooth comb, that I was just a pediatric nurse, and probably worrying too much. But deep down, I knew. Even though Patrick had great eye contact and smiled a lot, he didn’t move much and rarely made sounds. That combination stood out to me from very early on. ‍ What was your experience like navigating Early Intervention and specialist referrals before you had a diagnosis? Navigating early intervention and specialist referrals before we had a diagnosis was both a positive and exhausting experience. On one hand, we were lucky to have access to some truly wonderful therapists (physical, speech, and occupational) who were committed and compassionate. We also had the best of the best doctors, mainly in New York City. On the other hand, managing all of it was overwhelming. Coordinating everyone’s schedules, having multiple therapists coming into the house, trying to keep up with Patrick’s and the family's meals, Patrick's need for downtime, and caring for the rest of the family…it all became a full-time job. I felt like I was on the phone with insurance every other day. We had to make an important decision for me as a nurse, that I would only work 1-2 days a week, because it was just too much. It was a very hard and emotionally draining time in my life, even though I was grateful for the support we were receiving. ‍ How did you come to the decision to pursue genetic testing, and what was that process like emotionally? After seeing so many different specialists and still not getting any clear answers, I eventually realized there was only one path left to explore: genetic testing. Emotionally, it was a really difficult decision. I had put it off for a long time because the idea of a genetic disorder was terrifying to me. Unlike other diagnoses, genetics felt permanent, something you couldn’t fix with medication or therapy. The thought of uncovering something unchangeable about Patrick’s future was overwhelming. But after exhausting all other possibilities, I knew we had to face it. As hard as it was, it was the only way to start understanding what we were truly dealing with. ‍ Can you describe what it felt like to finally get the CACNA1C diagnosis? When we finally got the CACNA1C diagnosis, it was a strange mix of fear and relief. I was told at first that only 26 people in the world had it, and I immediately realized I wouldn’t be able to find much, if anything, online. But in a way, that was a relief. I had spent the past two years staying up at night, waking up at 3 a.m. with new search terms in my head, endlessly Googling things like “not talking yet” or “not doing this yet.” When the diagnosis came, my husband and I had a glass of wine together—not just to acknowledge that we finally had a name for what Patrick was going through, but also to toast the fact that I could stop Googling. ‍ Of course, the diagnosis itself was terrifying. A week later, I learned the number had changed; it was 46 people now, though still under 100. I had no idea what that meant for Patrick’s future. I was especially scared of the cardiac implications, though I felt a bit reassured because we had already seen a cardiologist and his heart was fine at that point. I was also worried about the possibility of seizures, since Patrick had this constant eye-rolling motion that made me wonder, but again, we had already done EEGs. In some ways, I was incredibly grateful that I had seen so many specialists before getting the diagnosis. It meant we had already checked off so many of the scary possibilities that come with CACNA1C. So while it was a frightening answer, it was still an answer, and that brought a kind of peace. ‍ What changed for your family once you had a confirmed genetic diagnosis? A lot changed for our family after we received the confirmed genetic diagnosis. At first, I didn’t do much. I think I was numb, maybe even a little depressed, without fully realizing it. I didn’t know what this diagnosis meant for Patrick or how I was going to change as a mother now that I had this knowledge. I was constantly afraid of something happening to his heart or him starting to seize. Even now, I still sleep with a baby monitor focused on his face, just in case. The rarity of CACNA1C means there’s still so much unknown, and that fear doesn’t just disappear. ‍ But a few months later, I finally gathered the courage to search “CACNA1C” on Facebook. That’s when I connected with Sophie, the head of our support group, who also has a child with a CACNA1C-related disorder. That moment changed my life. She told me I wasn’t alone, that she had a “Patrick,” too. I broke down in tears, shaking, crying with relief, comfort, and hope. For the first time, I spoke to someone who had walked in my shoes, seen the same specialists, felt the same confusion, and knew exactly what I was going through. ‍ Since then, our family dynamic has shifted significantly. I don’t work nearly as much anymore because this, supporting Patrick, managing this diagnosis, and advocating for others, has become my real full-time job. I want to make sure he has every chance to thrive, and I also want to help other families avoid the trauma and isolation I experienced. My hope is that, in the future, when a mom gets this diagnosis, she’s immediately met with information, guidance, and a community. I don’t want anyone to have to face the diagnosis in the dark like I did. ‍ How did connecting with Sophie, from the patient advocacy organization for CACNA1C, change your experience? Meeting Sophie, the mom who registered Timothy Syndrome Alliance (TSA) as a charity to support families with CACNA1C-related disorders, truly changed the course of my journey. She gave me hope when I didn’t even know I was looking for it. I admire her deeply, not only for how she supports her own child, but for how, even back in 2016, when there was almost no information available, she took action. After getting her child’s diagnosis, she connected with a researcher and immediately began building a community so that families like mine wouldn’t feel so alone. ‍ Sophie and I speak often, and I now serve on the board with her. I’m incredibly grateful to have Sophie in my life. That connection opened the door for me to meet many other parents going through the same thing, and it inspired me to start supporting others as well . As a pediatric nurse, I have the advantage of understanding the medical system and knowing which specialists to seek out, which is something many families understandably struggle with. I try to use that knowledge to guide others, both within our CACNA1C community and beyond. I’ve helped families with other rare and frightening diagnoses, and I often find myself offering support to parents I meet in the hospital. It’s become part of who I am now. I am someone who not only walks this road but also tries to light the way for others, too. ‍ How has your perspective on genetic conditions and testing changed over time? My perspective on genetic conditions and testing has changed dramatically over time. In the beginning, I was terrified of genetic testing. I was afraid of what we might uncover and how it could change everything. But now, I’m passionate about raising awareness and encouraging other families to consider it. I’ve come to realize that knowledge truly is power. Yes, getting a diagnosis is scary, but without that information, researchers and scientists have nothing to work with. If families don’t speak up, if we don’t share our stories, then no one even knows our children exist, let alone what their symptoms are, or how to help them. ‍ Because of genetic testing, I now know that Patrick is at risk for cardiac events and seizures. That knowledge allows me to be prepared. He wears a Holter monitor for two weeks every year to track his heart rhythm, and he gets three-day EEGs to monitor for seizures, even the ones I might not be able to detect on my own. If I had never pursued genetic testing, I would have no way of knowing these risks, and no plan in place to handle them if they happened. ‍ More than anything, I want families to understand that genetic testing isn’t just about getting answers, it’s about protecting your child and potentially opening the door to treatments or a cure. That can only happen if we are willing to step forward and share what we’ve learned. ‍ Tell us about Yammy, your service dog, and the role he plays in Patrick’s care and awareness journey. Yammy, our service dog, has been such an incredible part of Patrick’s journey. What a story! Even before we had a diagnosis, I remember asking Patrick’s neurologist if getting a service dog might help. I was hoping it could motivate him to move more, to engage. The neurologist said, “You’re dealing with something so rare—try anything outside the box.” So I did. ‍ By the time Yammy came into our lives, we had received the CACNA1C diagnosis, and Patrick was still not moving as much as he should have been. But everything changed once Yammy arrived. He completely motivated Patrick. Suddenly, Patrick wanted to walk, run, climb, and be wherever Yammy was. He started attempting stairs and even began using his right arm, which he had rarely used before. Playing fetch with Yammy became a kind of therapy. Patrick started throwing the ball with his right hand, and now he almost uses both hands equally. The dog gave him a sense of security and companionship that pushed him to try things he hadn’t before. ‍ What I didn’t expect, and what’s been so incredible, is how Yammy has helped raise awareness for CACNA1C. People are drawn to stories about service dogs. They’re curious and engaged, and that gives me the chance to share our story. Yammy has opened the door to so many conversations that wouldn’t have happened otherwise. He’s not only helped Patrick in amazing ways, but he’s also helped us shine a light on a very rare condition and connect with others. ‍ And something I still find unbelievable is that I applied for Yammy before we even had Patrick’s diagnosis. At that time, I had no idea Patrick was at risk for cardiac episodes or seizures. But now that we do know, having a trained service dog gives us an added layer of safety and peace of mind. God forbid something happens, we have a plan, and Yammy is a part of that plan. I had no way of knowing how important that decision would be, but it ended up being one of the best I’ve ever made. ‍ What advice do you have for parents whose children are showing unexplained symptoms, but still don’t have answers? My biggest piece of advice to parents whose children are showing unexplained symptoms is this: get genetic testing. One genetic counselor once told me something that stuck with me: if your child just isn’t developing the way they should, it’s simple. In most cases, it’s just a mouth swab, not even blood work. For peace of mind alone, do the swab. Make sure there’s nothing you’re missing. Leave no stone unturned. ‍ Of course, we all hope the results come back negative. But if they’re positive, then at least you know what road you’re on, and knowing that is everything. Because if you don’t even know the road exists, you can’t begin to support your child in the way they need. ‍ It’s also important for parents to understand that genetic disorders don’t always come with visible signs. Your child can look completely typical and still have a rare condition. They don’t need to have physical differences to warrant testing. And while pediatricians or even neurologists may not mention genetic testing, that doesn’t mean it’s not worth doing. You have to trust your gut. If something feels off, pursue it. You don’t need a specialist’s permission to advocate for your child. ‍ So many families receive diagnoses like autism, ADHD, or cerebral palsy—and those are real, valid diagnoses, but sometimes, they’re just one piece of a larger puzzle that only genetic testing can uncover. If your child has a genetic disorder, finding it early gives you the chance to monitor risks, seek targeted therapies, and connect with the right community. ‍ So again, just do the mouth swab. The answers might change your entire path, and could be exactly what your child needs. ‍ What are your hopes for Patrick’s future and other kids like him? ‍ My greatest hope for Patrick is that he is happy, healthy, and safe. That’s what matters most. I want him to be the very best version of his Patrick self, whatever that looks like for him. We put so much into his growth, from therapy to swim lessons to gymnastics, and I truly hope all of that continues to help him make progress. I believe Patrick is incredibly smart. Sometimes, because of his motor delays, it can be hard to see just how much he understands, but I know it’s all in there. Once we find the right tools to support his motor development, I think his knowledge will really come out. I can’t wait to see that unfold. And it’s not just about Patrick. I hope the same for every child with this diagnosis that they each get the chance to become the fullest version of who they are. I hope every family finds the support, resources, and community they need to help their child thrive. That’s what this journey is really about: believing in our kids and doing everything we can to help them grow into their own beautiful, unique futures. ‍ If you’d like to learn more about CACNA1C-related conditions, please visit https://timothysyndrome.org/ .

title: How Much Does an AI Chatbot Cost? 2026 Pricing Guide
summary: Real 2026 AI chatbot pricing: you can start free, and paid plans run $9 to $999 a month. We built one on the free plan and counted every real cost.
body_text: An AI chatbot can cost nothing to start and millions to build. Most businesses land somewhere in between, and the final number depends on a handful of concrete choices: how many conversations you handle, which AI model runs them, how many channels and integrations you connect, and whether you buy a platform or build your own. Here is the short answer. You can start for free. Several platforms include a free plan, and Quickchat AI’s gives you 50 AI replies a month with no card. Paid plans commonly run from $9 to $999 a month , and most small and mid-sized businesses settle on a plan between $29 and $99. Usage-based and enterprise plans are billed per resolved conversation, often from around $0.50 each . Building your own from scratch is a different order of magnitude : $5,000 to $30,000 for a simple bot, $75,000 to $500,000 or more for a custom AI bot, plus ongoing model and hosting bills. The rest of this guide breaks those numbers down, and then does something most pricing guides do not: we actually built an AI chatbot on the free plan and counted every real cost, so you can see exactly where the money goes. Chatbot cost at a glance Scenario Low Typical High Notes Start on a free plan $0 $0 $0 Enough to test and run a low-volume bot. Small business (subscription) $9/mo $29 to $99/mo $299/mo No-code AI platform, standard support use. Mid-market (subscription) $99/mo $299 to $999/mo $999+/mo More replies, channels, integrations, seats. Enterprise (usage-based) $0.50/resolution $1 to $2/resolution $6+/resolution Billed per resolved conversation. Build a simple bot (custom) $5,000 $10,000 to $30,000 $30,000+ One-time build, rule-based. Build a custom AI bot $75,000 $150,000 $500,000+ Plus model, hosting, and maintenance. Annual maintenance (custom) $1,000 $5,000 to $15,000 $20,000+ Updates, retraining, monitoring. Rule of thumb for usage-based pricing: budget roughly $0.50 to $6 per resolved conversation , which usually covers the AI, the platform, and some support. In this guide: How much does an AI chatbot cost? What makes a chatbot more expensive? Chatbot pricing models explained Is it cheaper to build or buy a chatbot? We built an AI chatbot on the free plan Hidden chatbot costs people miss How to estimate your monthly chatbot cost How much does an AI chatbot cost? AI chatbot costs run from completely free basic tools to enterprise builds topping $1 million . Here is a simpler way to look at the ranges by business type in 2026. Basic chatbot for a small or mid-sized business Low: around $9 to $30 a month on a no-code AI platform, or free to start. Typical: $29 to $99 a month on subscription, or a one-time build of $5,000 to $30,000 for a custom rule-based bot. High: $150 to $300 a month with advanced features, or build costs up to $30,000 . Handles FAQs, basic lead capture, and simple routing. AI chatbot for a mid-market company Low: around $99 a month on subscription for an AI platform with natural language understanding. Typical: roughly $299 to $999 a month on subscription, or a custom build of $75,000 to $150,000 . High: $999+ a month on subscription, or build costs up to $500,000 for advanced AI and deeper integrations. Handles personalized support, resolves complex queries, connects to your CRM or helpdesk. Enterprise generative AI chatbot Low to typical: usage-based from $0.50 to $2.00 per resolved conversation , which at scale often works out cheaper than a fixed high-tier subscription. Custom build: usually $150,000 to $500,000 . High: $1,000,000 and beyond for proprietary models with extensive data training, top-tier security, and complex integrations. Handles sophisticated multi-turn conversations, hyper-personalization, and internal knowledge management. These numbers are guideposts. Actual costs shift with vendor pricing, the features you choose, and how complex your build gets. The single biggest factor is the chatbot’s core nature: whether it follows predefined rules, uses AI, or runs on a large language model (LLM). What makes a chatbot more expensive? Beyond the pricing model, a handful of factors shape the total cost. Understanding these drivers helps you budget accurately and avoid surprises. The type of bot The core technology, the bot’s “type,” is the biggest cost decider. More intelligence and capability means higher development or subscription cost. Chatbot type Development cost Subscription cost (monthly) Best for Rule-based $5,000 to $30,000 $9 to $150 FAQs, basic info gathering, simple scheduling. AI-powered $75,000 to $500,000 $29 to $999+ Complex support, personalized answers, nuanced queries. Generative AI $150,000 and up Varies (often usage-based) Dynamic problem-solving, deeply conversational experiences. Runs on an LLM. If you want the deeper distinction between a wrapper over a general model and a purpose-built agent, see GPTs vs Quickchat AI: what’s the difference . Advanced features Each sophisticated capability adds development complexity and often pushes you into a higher subscription tier. Feature Additional development cost Notes Natural language understanding $20,000 to $50,000 Core of any AI chatbot. Multilingual support $10,000 to $30,000 To converse in several languages. Voice capabilities $25,000 to $100,000 Speech-to-text and text-to-speech. Sentiment analysis From around $15,000 Reads emotional tone for better responses. Transactional actions Varies Secure integrations for payments or orders. On a modern platform, most of these are simply included in the plan rather than billed as custom development. Multilingual support and personalities, for example, ship on every Quickchat AI tier. Integrations Chatbots rarely work in isolation; they connect to your existing systems. Custom API development for each connection can run from $5,000 to $25,000 when you build it yourself. Integration Estimated cost (custom) Notes CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot) $1,000 to $50,000 Customer history and personalization. ERP (SAP, Oracle) $20,000 to $110,000 Inventory, order status, financial data. E-commerce (Shopify, Magento) $1,500 to $25,000 Product recommendations, order tracking. Messaging apps (WhatsApp, Messenger) $1,500 to $3,500 per platform Often included on platforms; WhatsApp adds Meta per-conversation fees. On a no-code platform, most of these connections are one-click and included, so the “integration cost” is your setup time rather than a development bill. Branding and user experience Using a platform’s standard templates and flows is the budget-friendly path. A bespoke look, custom avatars, and tailored conversation design add roughly a 20% to 30% design premium on a custom build. On subscription platforms, removing vendor branding is usually a paid-tier feature rather than a development cost. For the exact steps to white-label an AI chatbot , including which parts are free and which need a paid plan, see our hands-on tutorial. Platform, in-house team, or agency Your build approach drives the cost more than almost anything else. No-code platform: pre-built modules and a visual editor cut development time to near zero. Plans range from free to a few hundred dollars a month. Best for most businesses. In-house build: maximum control, but significant recurring salary cost. Role Approximate annual salary Project manager $88,000 Chatbot developer $90,000 to $120,000 NLP engineer $110,000 to $140,000 UI/UX designer $80,000 to $110,000 QA tester $70,000 to $90,000 Agency: expertise and faster delivery. Project fees run from $15,000 to $300,000 or more, with retainers often starting around $5,000 a month. Support, maintenance, and hosting For a custom build, ongoing costs are recurring and easy to underestimate. Item Estimated cost Notes Basic maintenance $1,000 to $5,000 per year Routine checks, bug fixes, minor updates. Model retraining $2,000 to $10,000 per quarter Keeps an AI model accurate. Hosting and vector store Varies with volume Servers, databases, and storage for AI processing. Security updates $500 to $2,500 per month Protecting the bot and its data. On a SaaS platform, hosting, maintenance, and model upgrades are bundled into the subscription. Compliance and security Meeting standards like HIPAA, GDPR, or PCI DSS adds development, auditing, and sometimes legal cost. Annual recertification can run $2,000 to $10,000 for standards like HIPAA or GDPR. Neglecting compliance risks fines and reputational damage, so treat it as a required line item, not an optional one. Chatbot pricing models explained Vendors price chatbots in a few different ways, and each affects your upfront and ongoing cost differently. Subscription plans You pay a recurring monthly or annual fee for a platform and its features, usually in tiers that unlock more replies, seats, or capabilities as you grow. Tier Typical monthly cost Common features and limits Free $0 Core features, a monthly reply cap, platform branding. Good for testing and low volume. Small business $9 to $99 Full AI features, common channels, basic analytics. Mid-market $99 to $999 Higher reply limits, more integrations and seats, branding removal. Enterprise $999+ or usage-based Dedicated support, SLAs, security and compliance, built for scale. Subscriptions give you predictable costs and ongoing updates. Watch the limits on lower tiers; you upgrade as your volume grows. Usage-based pricing Also called pay-as-you-go, usage-based pricing charges by how much you use the bot, measured in conversations, messages, or resolutions. A resolution is a request the chatbot successfully handled. Costs run from a fraction of a cent to several dollars per unit. This suits businesses with seasonal traffic, because your cost tracks demand, but it makes monthly bills less predictable during spikes. For a deeper comparison of per-resolution versus per-seat models, see AI agent pricing models compared . Hybrid pricing Hybrid pricing pairs an upfront setup fee , often $5,000 to $30,000 , with ongoing usage fees. Regulated industries like finance and healthcare lean toward this model, because the setup fee funds tailored compliance and security work. Custom builds A one-time custom build gives you full ownership and can run from $10,000 to over $1 million . You own the intellectual property, but you are also responsible for all maintenance, updates, and infrastructure. Subscription platforms handle those for you but keep ownership of the core technology. Is it cheaper to build or buy a chatbot? For most businesses, buying is cheaper and faster. Building only wins at very large scale or when your requirements are genuinely unique. Buying means faster deployment and predictable costs; building means higher upfront investment and full control. Comparing subscription platforms The table below reflects list pricing observed in July 2026 . Always check vendor sites for current figures, since prices change often. Note that several platforms have moved to per-resolution billing for AI features, so the monthly subscription is only part of the total. Platform Entry tier (monthly) Mid tier (monthly) Top tier AI billing Quickchat AI Free ($0), Starter ($9), Basic ($29) Essential ($99), Professional ($299) Business ($999), Enterprise from $0.50/resolution AI credits per reply; see the full breakdown below. Tidio Starter ($24) Growth (from $49) Plus (from $300 plus usage) Per billable conversation; Lyro AI add-on from about $32/mo. Intercom Essential ($29/seat) Advanced ($85/seat) Expert ($132/seat) Fin AI Agent at $0.99 per resolution, billed on top of seats. Zendesk Suite Team ($55/agent) Suite Professional ($115/agent) Suite Enterprise (custom) AI agents included on every plan; automated resolutions $1.50 to $2.00 each above a free allowance. ChatBot.com Essential ($19/user) Growth ($79/user) Enterprise (custom) Per user seat plus $0.99 per AI resolution. One clear shift defines 2026 pricing: Intercom set the per-resolution template with Fin, and this year Zendesk and ChatBot.com followed, billing per resolved conversation rather than per seat. Tidio offers true per-resolution pricing only on its top tier. Per-resolution billing can make costs lower than the headline subscription suggests, or higher if your resolution rate is low, so model both scenarios before committing. Building from scratch Custom development offers unmatched control at a much higher and more recurring cost. In-house burn rate: a dedicated team (project manager, developers, an NLP engineer, a designer, a QA tester) can cost $400,000 to $700,000 a year in salaries alone, before benefits, tools, and overhead. Agency project fees: roughly $10,000 to $30,000 for a simple rule-based bot, $75,000 to $150,000 for a moderate AI bot, and $150,000 to $500,000 or more for advanced generative AI. For a worked example of a custom customer-service build, see how to build an AI agent for customer service similar to Klarna . Build or buy: a quick decision guide Factor Favor buying (subscription) Favor building (custom) Budget Lower upfront, predictable monthly fees. High upfront; lower long-run cost only at massive scale. Time to market Days or weeks. Months or years. Customization Strong for standard use cases. Full control over unique features. Technical skill needed Minimal. Significant in-house or agency expertise. Maintenance Handled by the platform. Your responsibility. Ownership Platform owns the core tech. You own the intellectual property. Choose buying if you need a solution quickly, have fairly standard requirements, or prefer predictable operating costs. Most small and mid-market companies fit here. Choose building if you have highly unique needs, require deep proprietary integration, need to own the IP, and have the capital and talent to sustain it. We built an AI chatbot on the free plan: what it really cost To ground all of these ranges in something concrete, we built a real AI chatbot on the Quickchat AI free plan and tracked exactly what it cost. The short version: the build itself cost nothing, and the only thing that counts against the plan is the number of AI replies you send. We created a support agent for a fictional small online plant shop, Fern & Petal. Here is what each step cost. Step 1: create the agent (free) Creating the agent, naming it, and writing its instructions is free and takes a couple of minutes with no code. This is the agent’s identity and main prompt. Step 2: load its knowledge (free) We added a few help-center articles: shipping and delivery, returns and refunds, and plant-care basics. The free plan includes up to 50 knowledge base articles , so a small business rarely hits the limit. Loading knowledge does not cost anything. Step 3: add an AI Action (free) We added one AI Action so the agent can look up an order’s status mid-conversation. AI Actions let the agent call a live API while it talks to a customer. They are unlimited on every plan, including free , so connecting the agent to your systems does not raise the bill. If you want to see exactly how an action is built, build a free AI agent that takes actions walks through the whole thing with copy-paste values. Step 4: what actually counts, the AI replies Here is the one thing that costs anything on a usage-metered platform: the AI replies . Each reply the agent generates spends one AI credit , and the free plan includes 50 AI credits a month . A conversation is usually several replies, so 50 credits is enough to test the agent and handle a light stream of real questions. There is a catch worth knowing before you pick a plan: testing your own agent spends the same credits a customer would. Every time you try it out, that reply counts. After building Fern & Petal and testing it a handful of times, the account had used 14 of its 50 monthly credits, most of them from our own test messages. What Quickchat AI actually costs When you outgrow 50 replies a month, here is the full plan lineup, with the real numbers. A conversation is several replies, so read the AI-reply column as your monthly capacity. Plan Monthly AI replies / month Knowledge base Team seats Remove branding Free $0 50 50 articles 1 No Starter $9 150 100 1 No Basic $29 500 300 1 No Essential $99 3,000 500 1 No Professional $299 9,000 1,000 3 Yes Business $999 30,000 2,000 10 Yes Enterprise From $0.50/resolution Usage-based Unlimited Custom Yes Two things make this simpler than most pricing pages. First, almost everything is on every plan, including free : all channels except the raw API, unlimited AI Actions, lead capture, human handoff, and analytics. Only three things are gated by tier, removing branding (Professional and up), exporting conversations (Business), and API access (Business). Second, advanced AI models cost more credits per reply and are available on paid plans; the free plan runs on the standard model, which is one credit per reply. Annual billing is ten months for the price of twelve. See the pricing page for the current details. So the honest cost of a working AI chatbot on Quickchat AI is $0 to build and test , and then whatever tier covers your monthly reply volume, which for most small businesses is $29 to $99 a month . Hidden chatbot costs people miss The sticker price is not the whole bill. A few costs sneak up on your total cost of ownership. Testing spends your allowance. As we saw building Fern & Petal, the replies you generate while testing and tuning count against your monthly quota just like a customer’s. Budget some headroom above your expected volume. Cloud and model bills on a custom build. If you build your own bot or use pay-as-you-go AI services, compute and storage costs fluctuate and traffic spikes can produce surprisingly high monthly bills. Generative AI has higher per-interaction compute cost than simpler models. The cost of a bad experience. A poorly designed bot that gives wrong answers, loops, or blocks the path to a human frustrates users and can increase churn and cart abandonment . Winning back a lost customer usually costs far more than the bot ever saved. The cost of not having one. Without a bot, you miss leads and questions outside business hours. A chatbot answers around the clock and captures leads overnight, which can save significantly compared with staffing humans 24/7. For more on cutting support cost specifically, see how to reduce customer support costs . How to estimate your monthly chatbot cost Estimating your budget is a matter of working through your real needs rather than guessing. If you want a quick number first, the free chatbot ROI calculator estimates monthly savings from your ticket volume and support costs. Then work through these six steps. Define scope and objectives. Decide what problems the bot will solve, who it is for, what tasks it must perform, and how you will measure success. Aim for a clear list of what it must do. Pick a bot type and pricing model. Rule-based, AI-powered, or generative AI, and subscription, usage-based, hybrid, or custom. This gives you a preliminary cost for the core platform. Estimate user and agent counts. How many customers will use it monthly, and how many internal seats will manage it. Seat counts drive subscription tiers on some platforms. Forecast conversation volume. Note the systems the bot must connect to and any advanced features. On a no-code platform most are included; on a custom build, price each. Add contingency and ongoing costs. Include a contingency of about 15% , plus maintenance, support, retraining, and possible tier upgrades. That maps to the $99 Essential plan (3,000 replies) with room to test, for a predictable $99 a month all in, no engineering required. Do chatbots pay for themselves? For most support and lead use cases, yes, and usually within months. A chatbot pays back through cost savings, extra revenue, and softer benefits like faster response times. Cost per chat: bots versus humans The clearest saving is support cost. A chatbot interaction is estimated at $0.50 to $0.70 , while a live-agent interaction typically runs $8 to $15. If a bot handles 1,000 questions a month at $0.60 each ($600), and human agents would handle them at $10 each ($10,000), the monthly saving is $9,400. Revenue, not just savings Chatbots also lift revenue: they capture and qualify leads 24/7, guide shoppers through a purchase, and reduce cart abandonment , and they can upsell based on the conversation. To measure it, track leads and sales the bot influenced. A simple ROI formula Use this basic formula: ROI (%) = (Net benefit from chatbot - Cost of chatbot) / Cost of chatbot x 100 A worked annual example for a mid-sized support bot: Line Amount Cost savings (24,000 chats/yr at $9.40 saved each) $225,600 Revenue uplift (10 sales/mo at $500 profit) $60,000 Total annual benefit $285,600 Cost of the chatbot (build plus a year of operation) $60,000 ROI 376% Your real figures will vary with volume and timeframe, but the pattern holds: for support automation, the payback is usually fast. Launch a minimum viable bot that solves one or two core problems well, then expand based on real usage instead of paying for features nobody uses. Try no-code first. For a first version, a no-code AI platform removes development cost and launches in days. Many, including Quickchat AI, have a free tier. Reuse existing APIs. Before commissioning custom integration work, check whether your systems already offer APIs or webhooks. Using them is cheaper and faster than building new connections. Right-size your plan. Review usage regularly. If you consistently use a fraction of your tier, downgrade; if you keep hitting the limit, a higher tier is usually cheaper than overage. Negotiate at volume. For large deployments, ask about volume discounts and custom enterprise pricing, which is often not listed publicly. Streamline conversations. Frequently asked questions How much does an AI chatbot cost per month? You can start free: several platforms include a free plan, and Quickchat AI’s free plan gives you 50 AI replies a month with no card. Paid plans commonly run from $9 to $999 a month depending on how many replies you need and which features you unlock. Enterprise and usage-based plans are billed per resolved conversation, often from around $0.50 each. Building your own from scratch costs far more: $5,000 to $30,000 for a simple bot and $75,000 to $500,000 or more for a custom AI bot, plus ongoing model and hosting bills. Is there a free AI chatbot plan? Yes. Free plans are common and are enough to test a bot and run a low-volume one. Quickchat AI’s free plan includes 50 AI replies a month, up to 50 knowledge base articles, all channels except the API, and unlimited AI Actions, with no credit card required. The main limits are the monthly reply allowance, the standard AI model only, and platform branding on the widget. How much does it cost to build your own chatbot from scratch? A simple rule-based bot costs roughly $5,000 to $30,000 to build. An AI bot with natural language understanding ranges from $75,000 to $500,000. Complex generative AI bots can exceed $150,000 and reach $1 million or more. On top of the build you pay ongoing costs: LLM API usage per conversation, hosting and a vector store, plus maintenance and retraining. What makes a chatbot more expensive? The biggest drivers are reply and conversation volume, the AI model you use, the number of channels, the integrations and AI Actions you connect, and time spent on human handoff. If you build your own, engineering and ongoing maintenance dominate the cost. On a platform, the cost usually tracks how many AI replies you send each month. How much does a chatbot cost for 1,000 conversations a month? On a subscription platform, 1,000 conversations a month usually falls inside a mid plan. On Quickchat AI, a conversation is several AI replies, so 1,000 conversations maps to a plan in the $99 to $299 range (3,000 to 9,000 AI replies a month). On per-resolution pricing, 1,000 resolved conversations at roughly $0.50 to $2.00 each is about $500 to $2,000 a month. A do-it-yourself build adds LLM API and hosting on top. Does testing the chatbot cost extra? On usage-metered platforms, testing your own agent usually spends the same reply or credit allowance a real customer would. Every AI reply counts, including the ones you generate while trying it out, so heavy testing eats into your monthly quota. Budget a little headroom above your expected customer volume for testing and tuning. Are AI chatbots more expensive than rule-based bots? Generally yes to build, because AI adds natural language understanding and model costs. A rule-based build starts around $5,000 while an AI build starts around $75,000. On subscription platforms the gap is much smaller: modern no-code AI platforms start free or from a few dollars a month, so buying an AI bot is often cheaper than building even a simple rule-based one. Is it cheaper to build or buy a chatbot? For almost every small and mid-sized business, buying a subscription is far cheaper upfront and faster to launch, often days instead of months. Building your own only pays off at very large scale or when you have unique requirements a platform cannot meet, because you take on engineering salaries, hosting, and maintenance yourself. How much does a chatbot cost per conversation? Usage-based and per-resolution pricing commonly runs from about $0.50 to $6 per resolved conversation, depending on the platform and the complexity of the request. Intercom’s Fin bills $0.99 per resolution, Zendesk bills roughly $1.50 to $2.00 per automated resolution, and Quickchat AI’s Enterprise plan starts from $0.50 per resolution. What hidden fees should I watch for in chatbot pricing? Watch for overage or per-resolution charges above your plan allowance, the fact that testing consumes your allowance, charges for premium support or specific integrations, setup and onboarding fees, extra seats, and data or analytics retention limits. If you build your own, the easy-to-miss costs are ongoing maintenance, model API bills, and retraining. Conclusion The cost of an AI chatbot spans from free to seven figures, but for most businesses the practical range is narrow and affordable. You can start for free, most small and mid-sized companies run a capable support agent for $29 to $99 a month , and the cost tracks something simple: how many replies your AI sends. Building your own only makes financial sense at large scale or with genuinely unique requirements. The best chatbot is not the most expensive one. It is the one that meets your goals at a price that fits, and the fastest way to find that number is to build one and watch what it uses.
